review_comments:
This looks like one you added for backward compatibility - do you mind also adding it to the return documentation? It would also be good to have a test for the return values from the boto version as a precaution - you could add something like this to the ec2_vpc_route_table integration test after https://github.com/ansible/ansible/blob/devel/test/integration/targets/ec2_vpc_route_table/tasks/main.yml#L493-L511:
```
- name: test route table facts
  ec2_vpc_route_table_info:
    filters:
      route-table-id: "{{ route_table_id }}"
    <<: *aws_connection_info
  register: result

- assert:
    that:
      - result.id
      - etc
```

Sure. I will add it to the return documentation. I already added a test for checking if `id` is returned [here](https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/63413/files#diff-ea65d1c9ceeb31fc1b20355ec26f4dbfR593). I will add a test to check if `route_table_id` is also returned.
Is there any sort of deprecation policy to remove `id` from the returned values to stay in sync with boto3? Or are we now going to have it returned forever?
The PR for `ec2_vpc_route_table_info` was merged earlier today - #63413
Should I add the test case in a separate PR or should I rebase this on devel (so it includes #63413)?

@prasadkatti Ideally the tests would be merged before porting to boto3, so if you don't mind making a second PR to get in first that would be awesome. I don't think a top level `id` is the only thing that changed between boto and boto3. Ideally there's be an assertion for each return value. I know that's tedious. `routes` and `associations` both seem to have more keys in the boto output here - https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/44966#issue-212382602 (that comment may be incomplete though, as there are no propagating_vgws - I don't know whether boto returned if they exist, and if so, whether those contents differ between boto and boto3 too).

We don't have a good way of deprecating return values at the moment, unfortunately. I left a comment here with some thoughts on that https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/62985#issuecomment-544986596. Feel free to weigh in if you have ideas!

Also, thanks for the pointer to the PR merged earlier. I guess the `id` case is covered. :smile: Most of the others may be too, but if you could check that all of the return values are accounted for within reason that would be appreciated.

I have a question about this. The `route_tables.associations.id` (boto) has changed to `route_tables.associations.route_table_association_id` (boto3). Are we supposed to maintain backward compatibility for all such attributes? That sounds like a lot of work. I can try to do that if required. But can't we just add a release note for this module to let users know that some of the return values for this module have changed?

We'll need a standard 4 release deprecation cycle to change the output, we always want to be sure we give people a fair chance to update their playbooks that may depend on return values or any other functionality. I haven't tested, but I would expect you should be able to set result.route_tables.associations.id to result.route_tables.associations.route_table_association_id before returning the result.  Then we would need the module RETURN docs and a porting guide entry to state that the return value is being deprecated.  #52518 has a good example of the needed docs.

Thanks for the pointers. I am trying to gather a list of differences between boto and boto3 return values. This is what I have so far -

1. `route_tables.associations.id` is now `route_tables.associations.route_table_association_id`
2. Some fields seem to be returned conditionally in boto3. Before, in boto, they were always returned and would have a null value wherever applicable. Examples include `route_tables.associations.subnet_id`; `instance_id`, `interface_id` and `vpc_peering_connection_id` in `route_tables.routes`.
3. `propagating_vgws` - seems like a new return value

I know what needs to be done for (1). Don't think any action is needed for (3). For (2), do we want to add the missing keys with a null value?

Also, the above list is the difference that I could find. There might be more.

I think it's better to set them to null if they always existed before - unknown key would behave differently than a key that exists but is set to a null value and we don't want to break things for people if possible. Thanks very much for diving in to this.

Hi @tremble, this is the part where we add some keys to the returned dict to make it backwards compatible. Boto always had these keys defined and they are set to None when necessary. Now in boto3, these keys are missing from the dict if they are not applicable. The 2 tests that I added ensure that we maintain backwards compatibility by always having those keys present in the returned dict. When these keys are added their values are set to None to mimic boto2 behavior. So what tests exactly do I need to add here?
You could add `default: []` here (since omitting means it is `None`).
